title: Bridged Restoration Playbook for Traffic Spikes and Noisy Neighbors
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview:
This playbook defines a pragmatic, low-latency response for incidents caused by sudden traffic spikes and 'noisy neighbor' behaviors that degrade Redwood inference performance for one or more tenants. It covers detection signals, a prioritized containment ladder, traffic-routing mitigations, customer/status templates, on-call responsibilities, game-day simulation steps, and post-incident follow-ups. The goal is to restore broad service health quickly while preserving data integrity and providing clear communications to customers and stakeholders.

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to degradation events where latency SLOs or request errors increase across one or more model-serving clusters due to imbalanced tenant traffic or noisy workloads (e.g., long-sequence bulk requests, high concurrency bursts, or runaway retries).
- Not intended for software-only bugs (see separate code-regression runbooks) or hardware failures where evacuation/repair is required.

Key service targets and SLO thresholds (for on-call decisioning):
- P50 latency target: <= 180ms (informational)
- P95 latency SLO: < 850ms (SLO)
- Error rate SLO: < 0.5% 5m rolling
- Degradation alert thresholds (auto-alert rules):
  - Latency p95 > 900ms sustained for 3m -> P1 alert
  - Error rate 5m > 2% -> P1 alert
  - Queue length > 500 requests on a node pool -> P2 alert

Symptoms that indicate noisy-neighbor / traffic-spike incident:
1) Sudden ingress increase from a small set of API keys/accounts.
2) Elevated KV cache misses combined with long tail latencies.
3) One or two model-serving pods/instances consuming >70% GPU memory or >85% SM utilization while others are relatively idle.
4) Retrying clients or reconnect storms visible in request logs.

Detection & initial triage (first 10 minutes):
1. Acknowledge alert and open an incident channel (Slack #ops-bridge-<incident-id> and create incident in PagerDuty).
2. Triage officer captures initial signals:
   - Top 10 source API keys over last 5 minutes (monitoring query)
   - Top 5 node pools by CPU/GPU utilization
   - Per-region request rate and P95 latency deltas
3. Decide containment vs. full mitigation based on blast radius. If impact is localized to a customer or a single node pool, prefer containment.

Containment ladder (ordered by safety & speed):
1) Rate-limit / apply ingress throttles to offending API key(s).
   - Short-term target: reduce offending client concurrency by 80%.
   - Command example (internal traffic-shaper):
     adminctl throttle --api-key <KEY> --concurrency 10 --duration 15m --reason "auto: noisy neighbor containment"
2) Apply per-account token bucket limits at the edge (NGINX/LB) and enforce burst/steady rates.
3) Move noisy traffic to degraded-capacity lane (lower-priority pool) and apply model-fallback if necessary.
   - Use routing tag: noisy-neighbor => route to low-pri pool
4) Temporarily scale up dedicated GPU workers if autoscaling is slower than needed (fast path only when containment insufficient).
5) Evict long-running KV-cache-heavy requests or cancel queued requests from offending sources.
6) If the noisy tenant is high-value and containment would violate contractual terms, coordinate with CS/AM for soft-limits and manual throttling.

Operational checklist (actions and owners):
- Triage owner (SRE on-call): run initial monitoring queries and populate incident channel with top metrics.
- Runtime owner (Serving team): validate node health and identify overloaded pods for isolation.
- Network/Edge owner (Infra): implement edge rate-limits and block rules if necessary.
- CS/AM (Customer Success): identify impacted customers and prepare messaging if public-facing.

Speed commands and monitoring queries (copy/paste):
- Top API keys by RPS (PromQL):
  topk(10, sum by (api_key) (rate(requests_total[1m])))
- Node pool GPU utilization (Grafana query): filter by cluster:_cluster and avg_over_time(nvml_gpu_utilization[1m]) > 80
- Cancel in-flight requests (internal):
  adminctl cancel-requests --filter "api_key=<KEY> AND duration>120s" --dry-run
- Apply routing tag to re-route traffic:
  adminctl route set --api-key <KEY> --route-tag noisy-neighbor --duration 30m

Traffic routing and isolation table (operators):
| Condition | Action | CLI / Dashboard location | Expected outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| Single API key >50% cluster RPS | Apply per-key throttle (concurrency cap) | Edge dashboard -> Rate limits OR adminctl | Offending flow limited; cluster p95 improves |
| Many small keys showing aggregate increase | Create rate-limit policy by org | infra-console -> traffic-policies | Aggregate load reduced, fairness improved |
| Specific node pool saturated | Drain new requests, move routing | k8s: cordon/evict + adminctl route | Reduce hot-spot, allow eviction to catch up |

Escalation matrix (time-boxed):
- 0–10m: Triage owner determines containment step; notify on-call manager if P1.
- 10–20m: If no improvement after containment, page Runtime owner and Infra lead.
- 20–40m: If still degraded and customer-impact >10% of requests, escalate to Head of SRE and CS lead for customer comms.
- 40m+: Consider wider mitigations: cluster-level Autoscale burst, redirect traffic to alternate region, or soft failover to Redwood Dedicated.

Customer and status communications (templates):
- Status page short update (public):
  Title: Degraded inference performance in <region> due to high request volume
  Body: Our teams are investigating elevated request rates affecting inference latency for some customers in <region>. We have implemented temporary rate limits and routing changes to stabilize performance. We will provide updates every 30 minutes. Impact: some requests may experience higher latency or receive transient failures.

- Customer-facing email/snippet (for impacted customers):
  Subject: Temporary throttling applied to stabilize inference performance
  Hi <CustomerName>,
  We detected unusually high request volumes originating from activity linked to your API key that contributed to broader latency increases in <region>. To protect platform stability we have temporarily applied a rate cap to your traffic for 15 minutes while we investigate. No data has been lost. If this disruption causes critical business impact, reply and we will prioritize a tuned mitigation.

- Internal incident update template (first 30 min):
  - Detection: timestamp + alert name
  - Scope: affected clusters / % of traffic affected
  - Actions taken: containment step and time
  - Next steps: further mitigations and owners
  - ETA for next update: +30m

Post-incident assessment checklist (immediately after P0 cleared):
1. Capture final metrics (p95, error rate, top API keys) for the incident window.
2. Identify root cause: spike pattern, client bug, abusive traffic, or valid workload change.
3. Determine whether new guardrails (per-key quotas, fair-share routing) are required.
4. If customer-caused, coordinate with CS for remediation plan and potential billing/credit.

Postmortem & remediation (owners & timeline):
- Incident author: SRE triage owner (write the postmortem within 72 hours).
- Required sections: timeline, detection, impact, root cause analysis, corrective actions, preventive actions, roll-forward plan, and verification steps.
- Priority remediation timeline:
  - Hotfixes (<=7 days): apply emergency throttles and improve alert thresholds.
  - Short-term fixes (<=30 days): add per-account rate limiting and traffic-shaping rules.
  - Long-term engineering work (<=90 days): routing fairness algorithm, autoscale policy refinement, and improved per-tenant telemetry.

Game-day simulation plan (quarterly practice):
- Objective: practice identifying and containing noisy-neighbor incidents without customer-impact.
- Roles to seat: Triage owner (SRE), Runtime owner (Serving), Infra (Edge), CS on-call, PagerDuty coordinator.
- Scenario outline:
  1) Synthetic traffic generator ramps a single API key to 60% cluster RPS over 2m.
  2) Monitoring triggers latency p95 alert and queue-length alert.
  3) Triage owner must identify offending key within 5 minutes and apply first containment step in 10 minutes.
  4) Serving team practices moving noisy traffic to degraded pool and validates that lower-priority pool degrades gracefully.
- Success criteria: mean time to containment < 15m and restoration of p95 < 850ms within 25m.

Validation and runbook retirement criteria:
- This runbook is validated if used during one real incident or two game-day exercises in a 12-month window.
- Retire when: the platform routing layer enforces per-tenant fairness automatically AND we have monitoring proving no single key can exceed 30% cluster RPS for 6 months.

Appendix A — sample PromQL and SQL checks:
- Top keys by 5m RPS (PromQL):
  topk(20, sum by (api_key) (rate(requests_total[5m])))
- Error rate (SQL for audit):
  SELECT api_key, count(*) as errors FROM request_logs WHERE status >= 500 AND ts > now() - interval '10 minutes' GROUP BY api_key ORDER BY errors DESC LIMIT 20;

Appendix B — quick reference commands (for SREs):
- adminctl throttle --api-key <KEY> --concurrency 10 --duration 15m --reason "noisy containment"
- adminctl route set --api-key <KEY> --route-tag noisy-neighbor --duration 30m
- adminctl cancel-requests --filter "api_key=<KEY> AND duration>120s" --confirm
- kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data

Appendix C — ownership & contacts:
- On-call SRE: ops-oncall@redwood.ai
- Serving runtime lead: runtime-team@redwood.ai
- Network/infra lead: infra-oncall@redwood.ai
- CS escalation: cs-escalations@redwood.ai

End of playbook.
